newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour MP proposes major welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour MP proposes major welfare reform.

text.p: The Labour member of parliament Frank Field, a key advisor to the opposition party's leadership, on Tuesday unveiled proposals for sweeping welfare reform.

Field's proposals include a new state retirement pension entitlement for all workers, a new care pension to cover residential or nursing care and a new unemployment insurance scheme to help no-job households win their share of new jobs.

The report, costed by the official financial watchdog, the Government Actuary's Department, says the proposals do imply increased costs, mainly due to the care pension, where the extra public expenditure cost would be some three billion pounds.

But additional pension savings would rise from one billion pounds in the year 2000 to six billion three years later. There should also be a decline in unemployment as a result of the drive to encourage work and reduce welfare dependence.

Field said the Labour party's finance team led by Gordon Brown had not yet reviewed the proposals. However, the Labour leadership has encouraged Field to develop radical proposals on welfare reform which can then be considered by the party.

Key points in the plans include the creation of a new insurance-based tax system. All earnings over 10 stg a week would be included and there would be no upper limit, although the removal of the limit would be matched by tax reductions.
Workers on 10 to 60 stg a week would pay a lower rate. The same tax framework would apply to employers and workers.
This tax base would initially be used to finance half National Health Service (NHS) expenditure, a new care pension and a new insurance against unemployment.

To cover half of current NHS expenditure, a seven pence levy on earnings over 60 stg would raise 18 billion stg, and the move could be accompanies by about an eight pence reduction in the standard rate of tax or equivalent tax changes.
The pension reform would aim to give every worker a minimum pension entitlement of two-thirds of previous earnings.
The proposals would come into effect in the year 2000, when the state earnings related scheme, SERPS, would be closed.

Then, workers earning up to 100 stg a week would be entitled to the current state retirement pension of 61.15 stg, those already in occupational or personal pension schemes would continue contributing.
But anybody earning over 100 pounds a week and not in a scheme would begin to save contributions for a second pension.
The role of coordinating the drive to universal pensions would be the task of a new membership-run Pensions Corporation.
A new tax savings account would be established against which savers could draw tax allowances of up to 6,000 stg a year, replacing direct tax allowances to pension contributions.
Other tax subsidies to pension schemes would remain in place, apart from the tax concession on lump sum payments which would start to be phased out ten years after the reform began.
A mutually-owned National Insurance Corporation would be established to organise the new care pension and the new unemployment insurance scheme.
The care pension, to pay for residential care in old age, would be funded by a charge of three percent on all eligible income, offset by a four pence cut in the standard tax rate.
The new unemployment insurance will be built on incentives rather than sanctions, with benefit eligibility after thirteen weeks in work rather than two years.

There will also be changes to income support to allow claimants below pensionable age to use their allowances as an educational and training allowance. Student grants would also become student loans, freeing 1.1 billion stg for expanding nursery and childcare facilities, Field said in his report.
